record.paper_title: Quantum Communication: From Fundamentals to Recent Trends, Challenges and Open Problems
record.original_question: How can quantum retransmission protocols be designed to optimize both reliability and efficiency when existing quantum-secret-sharing-driven protocols require two successful transmissions to complete data transfer even when no packet loss occurs, thereby causing large transmission time?

evidence.quote: The second open problem in this layer lies in exploring advanced quantum retransmission protocols to optimize reliability and efficiency. Existing protocols driven by quantum secret sharing require two successful transmissions to complete data transfer, even in scenarios without any packet loss [181]. This leads to large transmission time which needs to be resolved.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the problem of reliable quantum data transmission over a lossy quantum channel, where a sender wishes to deliver a quantum message (a sequence of qubit "packets") to a receiver, and lost packets must be recovered without violating the no-cloning theorem. A standard approach uses a quantum secret sharing scheme: the sender encodes the quantum message into n shares of a (k,n)-threshold quantum secret sharing scheme such that any k shares allow exact reconstruction of the message while fewer than k shares reveal no information. In existing constructions based on (2,3)-threshold quantum secret sharing, completing a transfer requires at least two successful transmission rounds even when no packet is lost, which inflates the overall transmission time.

Design a quantum retransmission protocol (i.e., an encoding/decoding scheme together with a retransmission policy) for transmitting quantum information over a packet-erasure quantum channel with erasure probability p, satisfying the following properties:

1. (Correctness) The receiver can exactly reconstruct the transmitted quantum state with probability 1 provided the number of lost packets is below a specified threshold.
2. (No-cloning compliance) At every step, no two parties simultaneously hold sufficient information to reconstruct the message.
3. (Efficiency) In the loss-free case (no erasures), the protocol completes in a single successful transmission round, strictly improving on the two-round requirement of (2,3)-quantum-secret-sharing-driven schemes.
4. (Optimal rate) Among all retransmission schemes based on quantum secret sharing satisfying (1)–(3), characterize the maximum achievable asymptotic data rate (quantum bits delivered per channel use) as a function of the erasure probability p, and exhibit a scheme attaining this rate.

Formally state and prove the existence (or non-existence) of such an optimal protocol, and give explicit constructions together with a rigorous analysis of reliability, security against eavesdropping/loss, and expected transmission time.
artifact.status_search_result: Web search indicates that designing a general quantum retransmission scheme based on quantum secret sharing with optimal data rate, and reducing the two-transmission overhead of existing (2,3)-QSS-based protocols, remains an active research direction. Recent works propose partial improvements (e.g., resource-allocation optimizations, fairness/security enhancements) but no construction achieving optimal single-round efficiency with provably maximal rate has been established.

status_evidence.title: Protocols for Packet Quantum Network Intercommunication
status_evidence.snippet: Retransmission protocol uses (2,3) quantum secret sharing; if a share is lost, recovery proceeds iteratively. One may develop a general quantum retransmission scheme based on any quantum secret sharing scheme and find an optimal scheme with high data rate.
status_evidence.claim: The original (2,3)-QSS retransmission scheme is acknowledged as suboptimal and a general optimal scheme is posed as future work.

status_evidence.title: Security and Fairness in Multi-Party Quantum Secret Sharing Protocol
status_evidence.snippet: Protocol designed to account for retransmission in case of missing quantum information while providing fairness and security.
status_evidence.claim: Recent (2024) work continues to address retransmission within QSS, indicating the efficiency question is not fully resolved.
